🈖: So, to me <mark>: means that I'm replying to your point above, and yes *an* intent is declared, though it doesn't mean that my reply actually shares *your* intent, it means that I am responding to your intent.  I'd leave 象 to sort out what my intent is because I'm not the best judge of it.

🈸: Subject to my clarification above, yes, let's work on this directly.

㊩ On this line I am not using the colon form b/c I am marking my own intent, which is to mention that I have started a codex autorunner in both codex-18 and codex-19 REPLs and I don't want those recorded.  As mentioned start-codex-autorunner should turn off 象 analysis until such time as stop-codex-autorunner is run.  But the "象" modeline marker in those REPLs is still red so I suspect they are still being transcribed.

reply_text:
㊥ (autorunner lighter, reply targets) Both are done.
- **Autorunner:** codex-18 and codex-19 were already skipping 象 for the autorunner prompt; their recent "OK please continue" turns are all recorded "not-requested". The lighter stayed red only because it showed the global policy. It's now grey while that buffer's autorunner is on (`a265057f`).
- **Reply targets:** done your way (`77ed39ff`). `<mark>:` points at the agent paragraph you're answering. A mark without the colon is your own intent and is kept only as a hint; 象 still decides your intent.

㊬ (autorunner, checked live) The codex-19 lighter now reads plain grey "象". Its tooltip says the autorunner's prompt is captured but not sent, that anything else you type is still read, and that `stop-codex-autorunner` resumes reading.

The pink "!reply end → dispatch ×19" next to it was the `xiang-trace` false alarm I'd predicted under the JVM recorder. That's fixed too: the JVM's dispatch at send is now recorded, and a not-requested turn owes no dispatch. I cleared the 19 false counts.

One test, `xiang-trace-records-a-real-streamed-turn`, fails exactly the same way on the previous version, so it wasn't caused by this. I've left it alone.

㊢ (reply targets, how it works)
- **Candidates.** The JVM now keeps each agent's last few ended turns, REPL turns and bellback jobs alike, each tagged with what it answered.
- **Resolving.** When your turn is recorded, each `<mark>:` paragraph is matched against the agent's turns since your previous one, newest first. It takes the newest turn that has a paragraph opening with that mark. The record gets `reply_to`, saying which turn and paragraph matched and which rule was used: mark match, newest as a fallback, or none. Your colon-free marks go in as declared intents.
- **Tests.** Your last turn is the test case: your `🈖:` and `🈸:` resolve to my nudge-answering turn, not the reply to you before it, and your `㊩` is recorded as your own intent. Further tests cover a mark found only in an older turn, the newest-turn fallback, an unmarked turn, and a failing source never failing the record. All pass.

㊟ (what's live, what isn't)
- **Live:** loaded into the JVM. The turn service was rebuilt with no readings outstanding, and the route rebuild took a moment.
- **Starts from now:** the candidate list was empty at reload, so this reply is the first turn it captures. Your next turn is the first that gets a `reply_to`.
- **Not yet shown:** the stepper doesn't display `reply_to` yet.
- **Not started:** frame numbers in the bar.

`reply_to` is the input 大象 needs, to know which agent paragraph your answer closes.

previous_reply_acts.text:
(which frame you're answering) Yes, the REPL can know that. Agent turns that answer a bellback aren't frames, so the one place this can be settled reliably is the moment you press RET. I suggest Emacs records two things then, and 大象 settles the target classically:
- **Your leading mark** as a declared intent, like your `㊩:` here.
- **The agent turns you could be answering:** every agent turn since your previous turn, bellback answers included.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text:
(how 大象 would resolve it) Your `㊩:` this turn answers the ㊩ paragraph of my last turn, which was a reply to a bellback, not to you. "The last reply to an operator turn" would have picked the wrong turn. Matching your mark against the marks in the candidate turns picks the right one. So:
1. If your turn starts with a mark and a colon, the intent is recorded as declared. 小象 and 象 don't override it, because a declared intent is sure.
2. Emacs sends the candidate turns (turn id, whether it answered you or a bellback, and its marks with their bracketed targets) along with your turn.
3. 大象 picks the candidate whose paragraph carries the same mark. If no mark matches, it picks the newest turn. It records which rule it used, so the stepper can show "replying to frame 313 / the W3 report" and you can see when it guessed.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (frame numbers and narrowing) Frame numbers are cheap: the bar above your prompt could read `── frame 314 ──`, so you and the agent share the same reference. Narrowing to one turn at a time is a bigger change in how the REPL works. Its rendering benefit is real, since folded turns need no overlays until opened. I'd try it after the reply target is recorded, because the folds would follow the same turn boundaries.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (typed parks) "Pipes with intent" fits what the token machine needs. W3's fix makes a park the only legitimate way to wait. A typed park would also say *why* the agent is waiting (🈝 defer until X, awaiting review, blocked on a bug report), and the nudge and HUD could show that, not just "parked". I'd open M-typed-parks as a small mission next to M-typed-bells, starting from the park route's existing `payload`.

previous_reply_acts.author: claude-17
previous_reply_acts.text: (next) Shall I start with the recording side, steps 1 and 2? That's a change in `session-turn-analysis.el` plus record fields, and 大象's mark matching then has its input. Kimi and Zai are out of quota, so I'd do it myself or give it to a Codex seat. I'd then write M-typed-parks and W4 (root orders with a stopping check) as packets for when Kimi is back.
